summary:
As a department of Colombia, Cundinamarca stands directly under the national legal framework, and the sources in the record carry no finding on law, enforcement practice or recorded incidents specific to this department. A visitor's expectations therefore rest on how the national rules apply and on the enforcement record documented elsewhere in the country.

Legal gender recognition runs through an administrative channel rather than a court. Since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on a Colombian birth certificate, with current options of F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero), and the process is notarial, requiring no surgery and no court ruling; the sources state that this route applies equally in Cundinamarca. Decree 0732 of 2026, signed by outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo on 9 July 2026, obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request and any simultaneous name change free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure. A Constitutional Court ruling of 4 February 2022 ordered the government to offer the nonbinary option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws. Since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia carry three gender options: male, female and X. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

The violence record available to a visitor is national. The sources count 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight more between February and April 2024, and a CNN article of 6 August 2025 covers a wave of attacks against LGBTQ+ people in Colombia following the killing of Sara Millerey. No source in the record places such an incident in Cundinamarca.
tangentialFactors:
The baseline against which this department is assessed is armed-group violence documented in other Colombian departments. A Guardian investigation of 30 July 2024 reports that armed groups in Caquetá gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers directed at trans women, and quotes an activist stating that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases.

Both sources available here describe national conditions and neither carries Cundinamarca-specific content, so they indicate the environment a visitor enters rather than the department's own record. The CNN article of 6 August 2025 is accompanied by Equaldex context and reports the national wave of attacks after Sara Millerey's killing.
localsOnly:
Residents of Cundinamarca change their gender marker at public notaries. Decree 0732 of 2026 sets a five business day deadline for completion, waives the fee for the first request and for a name change made at the same time, and keeps the change history out of public disclosure.

Notary practice has not been uniform. A 2016 report by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity.

Residents face the enforcement gap described in the national record: an activist quoted by The Guardian in July 2024 stated that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide and instead records the killings as ordinary cases.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses departmental ordinances of Cundinamarca, police or notary practice within it, or recorded incidents there. The departmental layer of regulation and enforcement remains unresolved on this record.

The retrieved CNN page contained only site navigation; the account of its 6 August 2025 article is drawn from the description in the inventory, and that article offers nothing specific to this department.

The Guardian investigation of 30 July 2024 concerns Caquetá and contains no Cundinamarca-specific information; whether transfemicide recognition or notary refusal practices have changed since the 2024 and 2016 reports is not established by these sources.
